## TL;DR

A cell keeps two nucleic acids because one job needs a durable archive and the other needs a disposable, reactive copy. DNA differs from RNA by one oxygen on the sugar, one base (thymine for uracil) and a second strand, and those three differences explain where each molecule lives and how long it lasts. After this module you can trace a gene from DNA through mRNA to protein, read a codon table, and predict what a single-base mutation does.
:::

Every living organism on Earth, from the bacteria in a hot spring to the oak tree in your park and the trillions of cells in your body, runs on two nucleic acid molecules: **DNA** and **RNA**. Underneath the jargon (nucleotides, transcription, codons, ribosomes) is a small and orderly information system.

## Blueprint and photocopy

Transcription writes a single-stranded mRNA copy of one gene (magenta), and only that copy crosses into the cytoplasm, where ribosomes read it in triplets and tRNA delivers the matching amino acids. - **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)** is the **long-term archival database**. It stays safely protected inside the cell nucleus, ensuring the organism's genetic instructions remain pristine across decades and generations.
- **RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)** is the **mobile operational messenger and tool**. It is transient, chemically active, and acts as the bridge that carries instructions out of the nucleus to the factory floor.
- **Proteins** are the **physical hardware**. They do virtually all the heavy lifting: digesting food, contracting muscles, fighting infections, and transmitting nerve signals.

## Three chemical differences

Both DNA and RNA are polymers composed of repeating units called **nucleotides**. Every nucleotide contains three pieces:
1. A **Phosphate group** ($\text{PO}_4^{3-}$).
2. A **5-Carbon Sugar ring** (Pentose).
3. A **Nitrogenous Base** (the alphabet letters: A, T, G, C, U).

```{=html}
<figcaption><strong>Figure 2 | The chemical difference between DNA and RNA is a single oxygen on one carbon.</strong> Every nucleotide is the same three-part assembly: a phosphate joined through the 5&#8242; carbon to a five-membered sugar ring (blue, the backbone), which carries the information-bearing base off its 1&#8242; carbon and links to the next unit through 3&#8242;&#8212;OH. Only the 2&#8242; position differs (magenta): DNA carries $-\text{H}$ there, RNA carries $-\text{OH}$. That hydroxyl is a built-in nucleophile that can attack the neighbouring phosphate, so RNA hydrolyses in minutes to hours while deoxyribose keeps DNA readable for millennia.</figcaption>
</figure>
```


| Feature | DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) | RNA (Ribonucleic Acid) | Why the Difference Matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sugar Molecule** | **2'-Deoxyribose** (Contains $-\text{H}$ at 2' carbon) | **Ribose** (Contains $-\text{OH}$ at 2' carbon) | The missing oxygen in DNA makes it chemically unreactive and resilient for centuries. The extra oxygen in RNA makes it flexible and reactive. |
| **Nitrogenous Bases** | **A**denine, **T**hymine, **G**uanine, **C**ytosine | **A**denine, **U**racil, **G**uanine, **C**ytosine | Thymine has an extra methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$) that protects DNA from mutation repairs; Uracil is cheaper for cells to synthesize rapidly. |
| **Strand Architecture** | **Double-stranded helix** (Two antiparallel strands intertwined) | **Single-stranded** (Folds into complex 3D loops, hairpins, and knots) | DNA's double strand provides an automatic backup copy on the opposite strand ($A=T, G \equiv C$). RNA can fold like a protein to catalyze chemical reactions. |
| **Cellular Location** | Confined to the **Nucleus** (and Mitochondria) | Synthesized in Nucleus, active in **Cytoplasm & Ribosomes** | Keeps the master genome insulated from cellular metabolism and degradation. |
| **Lifespan** | **Permanent** (Lifespan of the organism / centuries in fossils) | **Transient** (Minutes to hours, degraded after use) | Allows cells to turn protein production on and off dynamically. |

### The alphabet and base-pairing rules

DNA's stability and ability to replicate flawlessly depends on **complementary base pairing** discovered by Watson, Crick, and Franklin in 1953:

```
        Complementary Base Pairing Hydrogen Bonds

     Adenine (A) ═══════════ Thymine (T)     [2 Hydrogen Bonds]
     Guanine (G) ≡≡≡≡≡≡≡≡≡≡≡ Cytosine (C)    [3 Hydrogen Bonds - Stronger!]

In RNA transcription:
     Adenine (A) ═══════════ Uracil (U)      [2 Hydrogen Bonds]
```

Because $G \equiv C$ pairs share **three** hydrogen bonds while $A=T$ pairs share only **two**, organisms living in boiling geothermal vents (thermophiles) typically have genomes with high $G-C$ content to prevent their DNA from melting at extreme temperatures!

The rungs count hydrogen bonds &#8212; two for $\text{A}=\text{T}$, three for $\text{G}\equiv\text{C}$ (blue) &#8212; and because the triple bond costs more energy to separate, thermophiles that live in geothermal vents run $\text{G}$&#8211;$\text{C}$-rich genomes to keep their DNA from melting.</figcaption>

## From code to protein

The **Central Dogma of Molecular Biology** (formulated by Francis Crick) describes the two-step translation process that turns genetic letters into physical proteins:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph Step1["Step 1: Transcription (In Nucleus)"]
        DNA["Master DNA Helix"] -->|RNA Polymerase| mRNA["Messenger RNA (mRNA)"]
    end

    subgraph Step2["Step 2: Translation (In Cytoplasm)"]
        mRNA --> Ribosome["Ribosome Factory (rRNA)"]
        tRNA["Transfer RNA (tRNA)<br/>with Amino Acids"] --> Ribosome
        Ribosome --> Protein["Folded Protein Chain<br/>(Enzyme / Muscle / Antibody)"]
    end

    class DNA indigo
    class mRNA plum
    class Ribosome sienna
    class tRNA ochre
    class Protein olive
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef sienna fill:#6c2b27,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef plum fill:#48304a,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef olive fill:#5b6e34,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef ochre fill:#d69a2e,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

### Codons, the genetic code dictionary

The ribosome reads the mRNA strand in triplets called **codons**. With 4 possible bases ($A, U, G, C$), there are $4^3 = 64$ possible codons, which encode the **20 standard amino acids**:

- **Start Codon**: `AUG` (encodes **Methionine**, signals the ribosome to start building).
- **Stop Codons**: `UAA`, `UAG`, `UGA` (signal the ribosome to release the completed protein).
- **Degeneracy**: Multiple codons encode the same amino acid (e.g., `GCU`, `GCC`, `GCA`, `GCG` all encode **Alanine**), making the genetic code resilient against random point mutations.

### RNA is more than a messenger

Messenger RNA (mRNA) is the type most people have heard of, especially since mRNA vaccines, but RNA does several other jobs in the cell:

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    RNA["RNA Types in the Cell"]
    
    RNA --> Coding["Coding RNA"]
    Coding --> mRNA["mRNA (Messenger RNA)<br/>Carries copy of protein recipe"]
    
    RNA --> NonCoding["Functional / Non-Coding RNA"]
    NonCoding --> tRNA["tRNA (Transfer RNA)<br/>Molecular adapter carrying amino acids"]
    NonCoding --> rRNA["rRNA (Ribosomal RNA)<br/>The catalytic engine of ribosomes"]
    NonCoding --> Ribozyme["Ribozymes<br/>Catalytic RNA cutting & splicing molecules"]
    NonCoding --> Regulatory["Regulatory RNA (miRNA / siRNA)<br/>Controls gene volume & silences viruses"]

    class RNA indigo
    class mRNA plum
    class tRNA ochre
    class rRNA sage
    class Ribozyme rust
    class Regulatory olive
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef plum fill:#48304a,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef rust fill:#a04b2d,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef olive fill:#5b6e34,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef ochre fill:#d69a2e,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
    classDef sage fill:#95a87f,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

#### The RNA World hypothesis

Did life start with DNA or with protein? Neither can come first on its own:

- DNA cannot replicate without proteins (polymerases).
- Proteins cannot be manufactured without DNA instructions.

This classic "chicken-and-egg" problem was solved when scientists discovered that **RNA can do both**:
1. RNA can store genetic information like DNA.
2. RNA can fold into 3D catalytic shapes (**ribozymes**) to perform chemical reactions like proteins.

Over 3.8 billion years ago, life began in an **RNA World**. Later, life evolved DNA for superior archival data storage and proteins for superior mechanical and chemical strength.

## Key takeaways

- DNA is the archive: double-stranded, 2'-deoxyribose sugar, thymine ($T$), and it never leaves the nucleus.
- RNA is the messenger and the tool: single-stranded, ribose sugar, uracil ($U$), it travels to the cytoplasm and can fold into catalytic ribozymes.
- The one extra oxygen on ribose is why RNA hydrolyses in minutes to hours while DNA stays readable for millennia.
- The workflow is $\text{DNA} \xrightarrow{\text{Transcription}} \text{mRNA} \xrightarrow{\text{Translation}} \text{Protein}$, read three bases at a time from `AUG` to a stop codon.
- The code is universal: every human, animal, plant and virus uses the same 64-codon dictionary, and its redundancy is what makes many point mutations silent.

```{=html}
const geneticCode = {

  'CCA': { aa: 'Pro', code: 'Pro', type: 'special' }, 'CCG': { aa: 'Pro', code: 'Pro', type: 'special' },

  'GCU': { aa: 'Ala', code: 'Ala', type: 'hydrophobic' }, 'GCC': { aa: 'Ala', code: 'Ala', type: 'hydrophobic' },
  'GCA': { aa: 'Ala', code: 'Ala', type: 'hydrophobic' }, 'GCG': { aa: 'Ala', code: 'Ala', type: 'hydrophobic' },
  'UAU': { aa: 'Tyr', code: 'Tyr', type: 'polar' }, 'UAC': { aa: 'Tyr', code: 'Tyr', type: 'polar' },
  'CAU': { aa: 'His', code: 'His', type: 'basic' }, 'CAC': { aa: 'His', code: 'His', type: 'basic' },
  'CAA': { aa: 'Gln', code: 'Gln', type: 'polar' }, 'CAG': { aa: 'Gln', code: 'Gln', type: 'polar' },

  'UGG': { aa: 'Trp', code: 'Trp', type: 'hydrophobic' },
  'CGU': { aa: 'Arg', code: 'Arg', type: 'basic' }, 'CGC': { aa: 'Arg', code: 'Arg', type: 'basic' },
  'CGA': { aa: 'Arg', code: 'Arg', type: 'basic' }, 'CGG': { aa: 'Arg', code: 'Arg', type: 'basic' },
  'AGU': { aa: 'Ser', code: 'Ser', type: 'polar' }, 'AGC': { aa: 'Ser', code: 'Ser', type: 'polar' },
  'AGA': { aa: 'Arg', code: 'Arg', type: 'basic' }, 'AGG': { aa: 'Arg', code: 'Arg', type: 'basic' },
  'GGU': { aa: 'Gly', code: 'Gly', type: 'special' }, 'GGC': { aa: 'Gly', code: 'Gly', type: 'special' },
  'GGA': { aa: 'Gly', code: 'Gly', type: 'special' }, 'GGG': { aa: 'Gly', code: 'Gly', type: 'special' },
  'UAA': { aa: '[STOP]', code: 'STOP', type: 'stop' },
  'UAG': { aa: '[STOP]', code: 'STOP', type: 'stop' },

};

function runTranslation() {
  const inputEl = document.getElementById('dna-input');
  if (!inputEl) return;
  
  let rawDna = inputEl.value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^ATGC]/g, '');
  inputEl.value = rawDna;

  // 1. Transcribe DNA to mRNA (T -> U)
  const mrna = rawDna.replace(/T/g, 'U');
  document.getElementById('mrna-output').innerText = mrna.match(/.{1,3}/g)?.join(' ') || '';

  // 2. Translate Codons
  const codons = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < mrna.length; i += 3) {
    if (i + 3 <= mrna.length) {
      codons.push(mrna.substring(i, i + 3));
    }
  }

  const aaList = [];
  const chipsContainer = document.getElementById('codon-chips');
  chipsContainer.innerHTML = '';

  codons.forEach((codon, idx) => {
    const match = geneticCode[codon] || { aa: '???', code: '???', type: 'unknown' };
    aaList.push(match.aa);

    let bgColor = '#334155';
    let textColor = '#fff';
    if (match.type === 'start') { bgColor = '#059669'; }
    else if (match.type === 'stop') { bgColor = '#dc2626'; }
    else if (match.type === 'hydrophobic') { bgColor = '#1e3a8a'; }
    else if (match.type === 'polar') { bgColor = '#0284c7'; }
    else if (match.type === 'basic') { bgColor = '#7c3aed'; }
    else if (match.type === 'acidic') { bgColor = '#b45309'; }

    const chip = document.createElement('div');
    chip.style.background = bgColor;
    chip.style.color = textColor;
    chip.style.padding = '6px 10px';
    chip.style.borderRadius = '6px';
    chip.style.fontSize = '0.85em';
    chip.style.fontFamily = 'monospace';
    chip.style.display = 'flex';
    chip.style.flexDirection = 'column';
    chip.style.alignItems = 'center';
    chip.innerHTML = `<strong>${codon}</strong><span style="font-size: 0.8em; opacity: 0.9;">${match.code}</span>`;
    chipsContainer.appendChild(chip);
  });

  document.getElementById('protein-output').innerText = aaList.length > 0 ? aaList.join(' — ') : 'No valid codons';
}

function setDnaPreset(preset) {
  const input = document.getElementById('dna-input');
  if (!input) return;
  if (preset === 'insulin') {
    input.value = "ATG TTT GTG AAC CAA CAC CTG TGC GGC TCA CAC CTG TAA";
  } else if (preset === 'gfp') {
    input.value = "ATG AGT AAA GGA GAA GAA CTT TTC ACT GGA GTT GTC TAA";
  } else if (preset === 'sickle') {
    // Sickle cell GAG (Glu) -> GTG (Val) mutation
    input.value = "ATG GTG CAC CTG ACT CCT GTG GAG AAG TCT GCC GTT ACT TAA";
  }
  runTranslation();
}

// --- SIMULATOR 2: 2D ANIMATED DNA DOUBLE HELIX CANVAS ---
let dnaHelixAnimId = null;
let helixAngle = 0;

const baseColors = {
  'A': '#38bdf8', // Light blue
  'T': '#f87171', // Red/pink
  'G': '#34d399', // Green
  'C': '#fbbf24'  // Amber/yellow
};

const baseSequence = ['A', 'T', 'G', 'C', 'C', 'A', 'A', 'T', 'T', 'G', 'G', 'C', 'T', 'A', 'G', 'C', 'A', 'T'];
const compSequence = ['T', 'A', 'C', 'G', 'G', 'T', 'T', 'A', 'A', 'C', 'C', 'G', 'A', 'T', 'C', 'G', 'T', 'A'];

function drawDnaHelix() {
  const canvas = document.getElementById('dna-helix-canvas');
  if (!canvas) return;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);

  helixAngle += 0.025;
  const centerY = canvas.height / 2;
  const amplitude = 55;
  const spacing = 40;
  const startX = 30;

  for (let i = 0; i < baseSequence.length; i++) {
    const x = startX + i * spacing;
    if (x > canvas.width - 20) break;

    const phase = helixAngle + i * 0.45;
    const y1 = centerY + Math.sin(phase) * amplitude;
    const y2 = centerY - Math.sin(phase) * amplitude;
    const depth = Math.cos(phase); // -1 (back) to +1 (front)

    // Hydrogen bond rung
    ctx.strokeStyle = `rgba(148, 163, 184, ${0.25 + 0.35 * (depth + 1) / 2})`;
    ctx.lineWidth = 2;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(x, y1);
    ctx.lineTo(x, y2);
    ctx.stroke();

    // Base 1
    const b1 = baseSequence[i];
    ctx.fillStyle = baseColors[b1];
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(x, y1, 6 + 2 * depth, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.fill();

    // Base 2
    const b2 = compSequence[i];
    ctx.fillStyle = baseColors[b2];
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(x, y2, 6 - 2 * depth, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.fill();
  }

  // Draw continuous backbone strands
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#38bdf8';
  ctx.lineWidth = 3;
  ctx.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i < baseSequence.length; i++) {
    const x = startX + i * spacing;
    const phase = helixAngle + i * 0.45;
    const y1 = centerY + Math.sin(phase) * amplitude;
    if (i === 0) ctx.moveTo(x, y1); else ctx.lineTo(x, y1);
  }
  ctx.stroke();

  ctx.strokeStyle = '#f43f5e';
  ctx.lineWidth = 3;
  ctx.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i < baseSequence.length; i++) {
    const x = startX + i * spacing;
    const phase = helixAngle + i * 0.45;
    const y2 = centerY - Math.sin(phase) * amplitude;
    if (i === 0) ctx.moveTo(x, y2); else ctx.lineTo(x, y2);
  }
  ctx.stroke();

  dnaHelixAnimId = requestAnimationFrame(drawDnaHelix);
}

function initDnaVisuals() {
  runTranslation();
  if (dnaHelixAnimId) cancelAnimationFrame(dnaHelixAnimId);
  dnaHelixAnimId = requestAnimationFrame(drawDnaHelix);
}

if (typeof document$ !== 'undefined') {
  document$.subscribe(() => {
    initDnaVisuals();
  });
}
window.addEventListener('load', () => {
  initDnaVisuals();
});
setTimeout(() => {
  initDnaVisuals();
}, 250);
</script>
```
